newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - News and new launches.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - News and new launches.

text.p: Asian debt markets were busy on Tuesday, as a number of new launches and debt-related news enlivened the market.
A U.S. missile attack on Iraq in retaliation for that country's attacks on Kurds in northern Irag had no effect on secondary market trading in debt issues, traders said.
Among new issues, Guoco Group unit Fresco Resources launched a US$180 million floating rate note issue.
The five-year deal pays a coupon 80 basis over the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate. With fees, the all-in return is 95 basis points to top-tier managers.
Arrangers are Fuji International Finance, Banque Nationale de Paris, Bayerische Landesbank, BZW Asia, JP Morgan Securities and Sumitomo Finance Asia.
Another Hong Kong company, Guangdong Investment, launched a US$80 million floating rate note issue via Schroders Asia.
The deal has a five-year maturity but can be put or called on the third and fourth anniversaries. It pays a margin of 140 basis points over LIBOR and an all-in of 170 basis points.
Schroders has been mandated along with Tokai Asia to arrange a HK$500 million floating rate certificate of deposit for Asia Commercial Bank.

Beijing-based China International Trust and Investment Corp (CITIC) today launched three tranches of Samurai bonds worth a total of 40 billion yen via lead managers Nikko Securities and Nomura Securities.
Another ITIC, Guangdong ITIC, closed a US$70 million FRN.
South Korean banks Kwangju and Kyongnam each have mandated four banks to arrange US$50 million FRN issues. Both will pay around 50 basis points over LIBOR for three-year paper.
South Korea's Newmax International (HK) is in the market with a US$50 million FRN, bankers said.

Bankers also said that Cho Hung Bank is taking bids on three-year paper. Cho Hung is hoping to pay LIBOR plus 30 basis points, which would a few basis points tigher than its last deal, the bankers said.

Hyundai International Merchant Bank reportedly still is taking bids on its US$100 million FRCD. Bankers said the deal, which is for five years with a three-year put, is being discusssed at about 65 basis points over LIBOR.
South Korea today announced more financial liberalization measures, including a proposal to allow more overseas borrowings by Korean companies in order to ease domestic interest rates.
Korean firms now face few restrictions if money borrowed offshore is used for offshore projects, but offshore funding raised for domestic use is tightly controlled, bankers noted.
In other debt news, Moody's Investors Service downgraded Thailand's short term debt ratings.
The ratings cut was another blow to Thailand's financial markets, which have suffered as the country grapples with political and economic problems.

Secondary debt market traders in Hong Kong said Thai paper--particularly that of second-tier banks--has traded poorly recently, partly because of the country's woes but also because the deals were priced too tightly at the start.
Philippine bank paper also is turning slightly soggy, not because bankers are bearish on the Philippines, but because supply has increased sharply this year.

Bankers said Security Bank is considering a new issue, adding its name to Rizal Commercial Bank and Allied Bank, which are taking bids now. PCIBank already is fixed for a five-year fixed-rate bond, which it will launch via Merrill Lynch.
